title: Companionable solitude
hook: I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude (Walden 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sounds of Walden: a train whistle, bells through the pines, bullfrogs trumping in the dark. Your line was sounds. Which of your five sounds surprised you? Day one thousand two hundred thirty.

A rainy evening. No visitors. The nearest neighbor is a long walk away. For some people, that's a picture of loneliness. For Thoreau, in the fifth chapter of Walden, it's something close to good company. He calls the chapter Solitude, and he says, without any apology, that he enjoyed being alone. More than that. He says solitude was the best companion he'd found. It's a sentence that some readers find beautiful and others find a little suspicious. Today we listen to it carefully.
screen: `A RAINY EVENING, ALONE.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED SOLITUDE.` → `THE BEST COMPANION.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. Thoreau writes: "I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude." He uses companion and companionable side by side, on purpose. Solitude isn't the absence of company, in this line. It is company, and of a good kind. Second, the surprise. He turns the usual worry around: "We are for the most part more lonely when we go abroad among men than when we stay in our chambers." Loneliness, he suggests, isn't about how many people are near. You can feel it at a crowded party. You can be free of it in an empty room. He says solitude isn't measured in the miles between people. Third, the rain. Thoreau is honest that it wasn't always easy. He tells of a time, early on, when for an hour he wondered whether he needed people nearby to live well. Then, in a gentle rain, he says he felt suddenly aware of a sweet and kindly society in nature itself, in the pattering of the drops and every sound around his house. The loneliness passed and didn't return. Fourth, the joke. He also writes: "I have a great deal of company in my house; especially in the morning, when nobody calls." It's funny, and it's also exact. When nobody calls, there's room for the morning, the pond, and his own thoughts. His solitude was never total: he walked into town, and friends came by. But being alone, for him, was something to be glad of, not to be cured.
screen: `SOLITUDE AS A COMPANION.` · `LONELY AMONG CROWDS.` · `A SOCIETY IN THE RAIN.` · `COMPANY WHEN NOBODY CALLS.` · then, large: `COMPANIONABLE SOLITUDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: alone, gladly. Settle, and let the breath slow. For these two minutes, nobody needs anything from you, and you don't need anything from anybody. Notice what it's like to be your own company. Is it restful? Restless? Either is fine. Now see if you can treat yourself as Thoreau treated the rain: as company worth keeping. Let there be a little warmth toward the one who is sitting here. The bell holds the time.
Companionable solitude. Thoreau's claim in Walden that solitude was the most companionable companion he ever found, and that loneliness isn't measured in miles. Today's word.
Your line: companionable solitude. Today, if you can, give yourself an hour alone, on purpose: a walk, a meal, a quiet room. Not as an escape. As good company. Day one thousand two hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Some readers of Walden set aside regular time alone, walking or sitting quietly, and treat it as company rather than as loneliness, after the Solitude chapter.

trapdoor: what you thought: companionable solitude means liking to be alone.
what it means: solitude itself can be good company, and loneliness isn't about how many people are near.
what a scholar hears: companion and companionable set side by side, in a chapter that admits one lonely hour and a cure found in the rain.

sources.ref: Walden, ch. 5 'Solitude' (one hour of doubt; sweet and beneficent society in the pattering of the drops; solitude not measured by miles)

notes: Verify the three quotations word for word against an 1854 text (the 'company' line is in the same chapter; confirm it is Solitude and not Visitors).

Paraphrases to check: for an hour he doubted if the near neighborhood of man was not essential to a serene and healthy life; in a gentle rain he was suddenly sensible of such sweet and beneficent society in Nature, in the very pattering of the drops; solitude is not measured by the miles of space between a man and his fellows.
'Some readers find beautiful and others find a little suspicious' describes readers in general terms; cut if an editor wants it sourced.
'He walked into town and friends came by' is supported by Walden's own chapters (The Village, Visitors).
